verdict.rationale: Four independent corpora converge on one continuous body. In 1 Cor 15:4 the verb is ἐγήγερται, parsed in MorphGNT as 3XPI-S, perfect passive indicative: has been raised and abides risen. The same perfect form recurs across 1 Cor 15:12, 13, 14, 16, 17, 20 and the perfect participle ἐγηγερμένον in 2 Tim 2:8, so the settled risen state is the recurring lexical signature, not a one-off. ἐγήγερται is paired with the aorist ἐτάφη (was buried, 3API-S), binding the buried subject to the raised subject. Luke 24:39 names σάρξ and ὀστέον (flesh and bones) as present and πνεῦμα as lacking them, with the imperative ψηλαφήσατέ (handle me). John 2:21 glosses the raised ναός as τὸ σῶμα αὐτοῦ. Acts 2:31 locates non-corruption in his σάρξ. The crux 1 Cor 15:44 keeps σῶμα constant in both halves and changes only the adjective, ψυχικόν then πνευματικόν, so the verdict holds.

scripture.force: ἴδετε τὰς χεῖράς μου καὶ τοὺς πόδας μου ὅτι ἐγώ εἰμι αὐτός, then the imperative ψηλαφήσατέ με (handle me, 2AAD-P) inviting touch. The clause πνεῦμα σάρκα καὶ ὀστέα οὐκ ἔχει names σάρξ (N-ASF) and ὀστέον (N-APN, bones) as present in the risen Jesus and absent from a bare πνεῦμα. Naming the two physical constituents of a body excludes a non-physical reading.
ἐπέδωκαν αὐτῷ ἰχθύος ὀπτοῦ μέρος. The narrative supplies a physical proof, broiled fish handed over, that presupposes a body able to receive and eat.
λαβὼν ἐνώπιον αὐτῶν ἔφαγεν. The aorist ἔφαγεν performed ἐνώπιον αὐτῶν (before them) is an evidentiary act: eating in front of witnesses rules out a phantom or apparition.

Φέρε τὸν δάκτυλόν σου ὧδε καὶ ἴδε τὰς χεῖράς μου, καὶ φέρε τὴν χεῖρά σου καὶ βάλε εἰς τὴν πλευράν μου. The hand (χείρ) and side (πλευρά) are present as palpable objects, with βάλε (put, 2AAD-S) directing physical contact. The closing μὴ γίνου ἄπιστος ἀλλὰ πιστός ties tactile verification to belief.

Χριστὸς ἀπέθανεν ὑπὲρ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ἡμῶν κατὰ τὰς γραφάς. The aorist ἀπέθανεν (3AAI-S) names a bodily death. The framing Παρέδωκα ὃ καὶ παρέλαβον marks what follows as fixed received tradition older than the letter.

ἐτάφη (was buried, 3API-S, aorist passive) καὶ ἐγήγερται (has been raised, 3XPI-S, perfect passive) τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τῇ τρίτῃ κατὰ τὰς γραφάς. The perfect ἐγήγερται denotes an abiding result, raised and still risen, and pairing it with ἐτάφη binds what went into the tomb to what came out. A non-bodily resurrection would leave ἐτάφη with no function.
ὤφθη Κηφᾷ, εἶτα τοῖς δώδεκα. The aorist passive ὤφθη (was seen, was visible to) with named human witnesses presents the risen one as seen by specific persons.

ἔπειτα ὤφθη ἐπάνω πεντακοσίοις ἀδελφοῖς ἐφάπαξ, ἐξ ὧν οἱ πλείονες μένουσιν ἕως ἄρτι. Noting that most of the five hundred remain alive at writing functions as a falsifiable check that presupposes physical visibility.

σπείρεται σῶμα ψυχικόν, ἐγείρεται σῶμα πνευματικόν. MorphGNT parses σῶμα as N-NSN in both halves and ψυχικόν, πνευματικόν as A-NSN attributive adjectives. The noun σῶμα is constant: only the adjective changes. In MACULA Louw-Nida both adjectives sit in the same domain 79 (features of objects), ψυχικός at 79.2 and πνευματικός at 79.3, so each names a quality OF the body, not its substance. πνευματικόν specifies a Spirit-animated mode, not an immaterial one.
Λύσατε τὸν ναὸν τοῦτον καὶ ἐν τρισὶν ἡμέραις ἐγερῶ αὐτόν. Jesus pairs ναός with a future active ἐγερῶ (I will raise) governed by a personal subject. The three-day frame matches 1 Cor 15:4.

ἐκεῖνος δὲ ἔλεγεν περὶ τοῦ ναοῦ τοῦ σώματος αὐτοῦ. The narrator's gloss places ναός (N-GSM) in apposition to τὸ σῶμα αὐτοῦ (N-GSN), fixing the referent of the raising as his body, not a community or a metaphor.

προϊδὼν ἐλάλησεν περὶ τῆς ἀναστάσεως τοῦ χριστοῦ, ὅτι οὔτε ἐγκατελείφθη εἰς ᾅδην οὔτε ἡ σὰρξ αὐτοῦ εἶδεν διαφθοράν. Peter cites Psalm 16 and locates non-corruption in σάρξ (N-NSF, flesh), naming flesh as what was kept from διαφθορά. The argument is incoherent if the resurrection is non-bodily.

complicating_texts.resolution: Read as denying bodiliness, σῶμα πνευματικόν would set the resurrection body against the physical. But MorphGNT parses σῶμα identically (N-NSN) in both clauses of v.44, and ψυχικόν, πνευματικόν as attributive adjectives (A-NSN) qualifying that same noun. In MACULA Louw-Nida both adjectives occupy domain 79 (features of objects), ψυχικός 79.2 and πνευματικός 79.3, while σῶμα stays in domain 8 (body). So πνευματικόν names a quality of the body, its animating principle, not its material absence. v.45 confirms this by glossing πνεῦμα as ζῳοποιοῦν (life-giving), Spirit-empowerment rather than immateriality. The same body that was sown is raised, now Spirit-governed.

σὰρξ καὶ αἷμα βασιλείαν θεοῦ κληρονομῆσαι οὐ δύναται. The phrase σὰρξ καὶ αἷμα is a fixed idiom for mortal corruptible humanity, set in parallel with φθορὰ ἀφθαρσίαν οὐ κληρονομεῖ in the same verse. The point is transformation of the body, not its abandonment. vv.52 to 54 keep the same subject, this corruptible and this mortal, putting on incorruption and immortality.

θανατωθεὶς μὲν σαρκὶ ζῳοποιηθεὶς δὲ πνεύματι. The datives σαρκί and πνεύματι function as datives of sphere or means, contrasting the mode of death with the mode of vivification, not body with disembodiment. Read with 1 Cor 15:4 and Acts 2:31, where σάρξ is preserved and ἐγήγερται is perfect, the parallel does not overturn bodily resurrection.

ἄφαντος ἐγένετο ἀπ' αὐτῶν, he vanished from them. A reading might take sudden disappearance and the locked-door entry of John 20:19 as proof of a non-physical body. But these texts describe new modes of operation of the same body whose flesh, bones, wounds, and eating are affirmed in the immediate context (Luke 24:39 to 43). New capacities of a body are not the negation of a body.

variant_units_examined.note: The longer ending of Mark (vv.9 to 20) is absent from the oldest uncials and bracketed in critical editions. It narrates post-resurrection appearances and would support the verdict. The verdict does not rest on it. Luke 24:39 to 43, John 20:27, John 2:19 to 21, Acts 2:31, and 1 Cor 15:3 to 8 are textually secure and independently sufficient. The perfect ἐγηγερμένον at Mark 16:14 matches the perfect pattern seen in 1 Cor 15 and 2 Tim 2:8 but is not needed.

Luke 24:40 (καὶ τοῦτο εἰπὼν ἔδειξεν αὐτοῖς τὰς χεῖρας καὶ τοὺς πόδας) was classed by some earlier editors as a Western non-interpolation but is retained on broad attestation. Even if omitted, v.39's σάρκα καὶ ὀστέα and vv.42 to 43's eating carry the verdict.
Some witnesses read ἕνδεκα (eleven) for δώδεκα (twelve) at 1 Cor 15:5 because Judas is dead. The variant changes the witness count, not the fact of bodily appearance carried by ὤφθη.

variants.note: All anchor verses fall outside the ingested ECM window (3 John 1.1 to 1.15), so not_in_ecm_scope holds and no CBGM apparatus was examined for them. NT data outside 3 John remains ECM-shadow for this project. Mark 16:9 to 20 is the principal adjacent variant, examined and judged non-load-bearing.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Its strongest case is real: ὤφθη (was seen) can describe visionary appearances, σῶμα πνευματικόν in 1 Cor 15:44 sounds non-physical, and 1 Pet 3:18 sets σαρκί against πνεύματι. Stated fairly, this reading takes the appearances as Spirit-perceived rather than tactile. But it must absorb σάρξ and ὀστέον in Luke 24:39 with the imperative ψηλαφήσατέ, the eating of fish (Luke 24:42 to 43), the side and hand offered for touch in John 20:27, the σῶμα gloss at John 2:21, and Acts 2:31's flesh that saw no corruption. The lexical weight resists it.

Stated at its strongest, this reads ἐγείρω of the believing community rising in faith, drawing on the metaphorical naos. But ἐτάφη paired with the perfect ἐγήγερται in 1 Cor 15:4 keeps one buried-and-raised subject, the named individual witnesses Cephas, the twelve, James, the five hundred (1 Cor 15:5 to 7) are persons not a corporate body, and John 2:21 supplies the explicit σῶμα gloss. The words do not support a purely corporate referent.

The same σῶμα that died is raised and transformed: 1 Cor 15:44's constant noun with shifting adjective, and 1 Cor 15:52 to 54 (this corruptible puts on incorruption), describe change of quality not of substance. Luke 24 and John 20 show continuity with the crucified body (flesh, bones, wounds) while Luke 24:31 and John 20:19 show new modes of operation. The proposition's clause now glorified, not merely spiritual, fits this lexical pattern.

hermeneutics.notes: A grammatico-historical reading of the four anchor corpora yields one pattern. The received formula of 1 Cor 15:3 to 8 supplies the earliest datable summary, and the perfect ἐγήγερται recurs through the chapter as its keynote.

stem_audit.notes: The stem names the contested distinctive (same physical body that was crucified, now glorified, not merely spiritual) without importing a tradition's proprietary vocabulary. The verdict is derived from the original stem. The clause now glorified harmonizes Luke 24, John 20, and 1 Cor 15:44 to 54 without preloading the outcome.

lay_summary: The Greek says the same thing across four independent corpora. In Luke 24:39 Jesus tells the disciples to handle him and look at his hands and feet, then names the two parts of a body, flesh (sarx) and bones (osteon), as what he has and a mere spirit (pneuma) does not. Verses 42 to 43 add that he took broiled fish and ate it in front of them. In John 20:27 he tells Thomas to put his finger on his hands and his hand into his side. In John 2:21 the narrator stops to tell the reader directly that when Jesus said raise this temple he meant the temple of his body (soma). In Acts 2:31 Peter quotes Psalm 16 and places the rescue from corruption in his flesh. In 1 Corinthians 15:3 to 8 Paul cites a creed older than the letter, joining was buried to has been raised, then lists named witnesses, noting that most of the five hundred are still alive to be asked. The one verb worth seeing is in verse 4: has been raised is a perfect tense, which in Greek means raised and still risen, an abiding state, and Paul repeats that exact perfect form seven times in the chapter. Now the hard verse. In verse 44 Paul calls the resurrection body spiritual, soma pneumatikon, against a natural body, soma psychikon. This is where readers split, because spiritual can sound non-physical. But the noun body does not change between the two phrases. Only the adjective changes, and in the lexical databases both adjectives, natural and spiritual, belong to the same category of words that describe a quality of a thing, not its material. So spiritual here means Spirit-powered and animated, the way verse 45 calls it life-giving, not bodiless. The flesh-and-blood that cannot inherit in verse 50 is corruptible flesh, transformed in verses 52 to 54 into incorruption. One body: dead, buried, raised, transformed.
